steps.title: Three sub-zones
steps.body: Rioja runs along the Ebro river in northern Spain. It has three sub-zones: Rioja Alta and Rioja Alavesa, cooler and higher, with Atlantic influence, and Rioja Oriental, formerly Rioja Baja, warmer and Mediterranean. Tempranillo leads, with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo, which is Carignan. Whites use Viura.

steps.title: Traditional and modern
steps.body: Traditional Rioja blends grapes from across sub-zones and ages them long in used American oak, giving pale, mellow wines with vanilla and dried fruit. Since the 1990s, modern producers have used French oak, riper fruit, shorter ageing and single vineyards, giving darker, fruitier wines. Both styles thrive today.
steps.highlight: American oak and time, or French oak and fruit

steps.prompt: Which sub-zone of Rioja is warmest and most Mediterranean?
steps.explanation: Rioja Oriental, to the east, is warmer and drier, suiting Garnacha.

steps.title: Navarra
steps.body: Navarra, just north-east of Rioja, was long known for Garnacha rosado. Today it makes reds from Tempranillo, Garnacha and Bordeaux grapes, and fresh whites. Its climate runs from Atlantic in the north to dry Mediterranean in the south.

steps.prompt: Which grapes are permitted in red Rioja?
steps.explanation: Nebbiolo is a Piedmont grape. Rioja's reds use Tempranillo, Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Rioja has three sub-zones and is led by Tempranillo
Traditional Rioja uses American oak and long ageing; modern uses French oak
Navarra moved from rosado to varied reds and whites
